extracted.intended_audience: citizens of New York; readers interested in constitutional design and public policy
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for designing the chief executive in a republican constitution (unity, term, powers, accountability, support, and relation to legislature/people). Aimed at assessing institutional arrangements that produce an 'energetic' yet 'safe' executive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ingredients of Executive energy
rubrics_metrics.description: The ingredients which constitute energy in the Executive are, first, unity; secondly, duration; thirdly, an adequate provision for its support; fourthly, competent powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is presented as a compact checklist of the necessary features for an 'energetic' executive; each ingredient is discussed in the text with supporting argument and examples. Use this list as the primary design checklist for executive vigor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ingredients of republican safety
rubrics_metrics.description: The ingredients which constitute safety in the republican sense are, first, a due dependence on the people, secondly, a due responsibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Safety criteria are intended to balance the energy ingredients. 'Due dependence' and 'due responsibility' must be combined with energy to make a stable republican executive; the essay discusses how to reconcile these.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of the Executive
rubrics_metrics.description: Unity is conducive to energy: decision, activity, secrecy, and despatch will generally characterize the proceedings of one man in a much more eminent degree than the proceedings of any greater number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text argues that unity should not be destroyed by plurality (multiple magistrates) nor by an ostensible single executive subject to controlling counsellors. Historical examples (Roman Consuls, Achaean Praetors) and state constitutions are used to illustrate harms from plurality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid plurality / single executive preferred
rubrics_metrics.description: Plurality in the Executive (either multiple magistrates of equal dignity or an ostensibly single executive bound to a council) tends to produce dissension, weaken authority, impede decisive action, and may split the community into factions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument includes risks: impeded measures during emergencies, rivalries, personal emulation, factional splits, and the inability to act with vigor. Examples and anti-patterns include Roman Consuls and state executive councils; the reader should prefer single-executive arrangements to maximize energy and avoid these pathologies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear responsibility and accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: Responsibility (both to censure and to punishment) is essential; multiplication of the Executive tends to conceal faults and destroy responsibility, making it difficult to determine who is blameworthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay emphasizes electoral accountability as particularly important: a single person is a clear focus for public censure and for removal/punishment when necessary. Anti-patterns: diffusing blame among a council, using 'I was overruled by my council' as excuse; collusion and mutually shifting accusations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independence from the legislature
rubrics_metrics.description: The partition of powers requires the executive to be independent of the legislative body; if the executive is dependent on the legislature, separation is nominal and the legislative may absorb all power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short executive terms or mechanisms that make the executive beholden to the legislature (or to legislative-majority influence over reelection) undermine independence. The text warns that popular assemblies may act imperiously toward other departments; constitutional design should protect executive autonomy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duration in office (term length)
rubrics_metrics.description: Duration in office relates to personal firmness in using constitutional powers and to the stability of the administration; longer duration increases the probability of firmness and independent action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A sufficiently long but limited term (discussion centers on four years as a reasonable example) gives the magistrate time to act with firmness and to establish reputation; excessively short terms create feebleness and improvisation. Use term length to balance independence with accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequate re-eligibility (ability to be re-elected)
rubrics_metrics.description: Re-eligibility is tied to stability of administration: the possibility of re-election gives incentives to good behavior and permits the community to retain experienced, approved magistrates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excluding a person permanently or temporarily from re-office reduces incentives to do good, tempts corruption/usurpation, robs the community of accumulated experience, and forces mutability of measures. Design options should allow re-eligibility to preserve continuity and reward merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control over appointments and administrative deputies
rubrics_metrics.description: Persons who manage executive details (foreign negotiations, finance plans, army/navy arrangements, disbursement of public monies) ought to be assistants or deputies of the chief magistrate, deriving offices from his appointment or nomination and subject to his superintendence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Linking subordinates to the chief magistrate promotes coherent administration and stability; dispersing appointment power away from the executive encourages mutability and undermines responsibility for administration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stability and continuity of administration
rubrics_metrics.description: Stability of the system of administration—avoiding disgraceful and ruinous mutability in administration—is essential for good governance and for allowing long-range policies to mature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frequent turnover and wholesale replacement of subordinate officers lead to mutability of measures and loss of institutional experience. Stability is especially valuable in emergencies (war, crisis) where experience and continuity matter greatly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequate provision for the Executive's support
rubrics_metrics.description: An adequate provision for its support (financial security/salary) is one of the ingredients constituting executive energy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adequate, secure compensation reduces temptations to peculation and corruption. The text notes expense concerns for councils (salaries, travel/residence) as an argument against plurality; ensure support is sufficient but not a vehicle for corruption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competent constitutional powers for execution
rubrics_metrics.description: The executive must be vested with 'competent powers'—the authorities necessary to execute public measures effectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Powers must be adequate to the duties of administration (war conduct, foreign negotiation, finance) so that the executive can act with vigor; however, they must be balanced by dependence on the people and responsibility to prevent abuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single object for public vigilance (concentrated accountability)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is far more safe that there should be a single object for the jealousy and watchfulness of the people; multiplication of the Executive makes confinement of executive power more difficult.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concentrated responsibility makes public opinion and scrutiny more effective; design an executive structure that leaves a clear, single target for popular vigilance instead of diffusing accountability across multiple actors.
